VBO:0201052.summary: Miniature Poodles are alert, loyal companions noted for how readily they learn. The breed’s older work involved wildfowling, and its French name caniche comes from cane, the word for a female duck; over time, Poodles became prized companions for their friendly, joyful nature.
VBO:0201052.shortDescription: An alert, loyal miniature Poodle from a French breed once used to retrieve wildfowl.
VBO:0201052.historicalRoots: French Poodle tradition, originally used for wildfowling and later prized as a companion.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 172: Poodle
sources.evidence: FCI documents loyalty/trainability, older wildfowling use, the caniche/cane name, Miniature size 28–35 cm and reduced-Medium proportions, plus solid black color. Character is breed-wide, not color-specific.

VBO:0201057.summary: Standard Poodles combine a joyful, friendly manner with quick learning and strong loyalty. Their older work involved wildfowling, and the breed descends from the Barbet. Even the French name caniche recalls that watery past: cane means a female duck.
VBO:0201057.shortDescription: A joyful, trainable standard Poodle with roots in the French waterfowling tradition.
VBO:0201057.historicalRoots: French Poodle lineage from the Barbet, with older wildfowling use and modern companion role.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 172: Poodle
sources.evidence: FCI traces Barbet ancestry, wildfowling history, friendly/joyful/loyal trainable character, Standard height over 45–60 cm with tolerance, and Standard as enlarged Medium. White is an allowed solid color. No color-specific temperament claim.

VBO:0201079.summary: Curly-coated Portuguese Water Dogs are spirited, intelligent workers known for courage and stamina. Traditionally they accompanied fishermen, retrieving escaped fish, helping when nets or lines broke, and even carrying messages between boats and shore.
VBO:0201079.shortDescription: A spirited Portuguese fisherman’s helper with a short, dense curly coat and a strong swimming past.
VBO:0201079.historicalRoots: Portuguese coastal fishing assistant, later concentrated in the Algarve region.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 37: Portuguese Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI describes intelligence, courage, resistance to fatigue, fish/net/line retrieval and boat-to-shore liaison; records two coats including shorter dense cylindrical curls and coastal/Algarve history. No coat-specific behavior claim.

VBO:0201153.summary: Smooth-haired Russian Toys are active, cheerful companions, curious about the world around them and strongly devoted to their people. Midcentury Russian breeders rebuilt a declining toy-terrier population and developed a breed distinct from its English ancestor. A 1958 litter from smooth-haired parents later produced the fringe-eared line that became the longhaired variety.
VBO:0201153.shortDescription: An active, curious Russian companion whose smooth-coated line helped give rise to the fringed variety.
VBO:0201153.historicalRoots: Russian toy-terrier revival from the mid-1950s; smooth-haired dogs preceded the longhaired line.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 352: Russian Toy
sources.evidence: FCI documents active/cheerful/curious/devoted breed character, 1920–50 decline and mid-1950s Russian revival, a 1958 smooth-parent litter behind longhaired variety, short close smooth coat and black-and-tan color. No coat-specific temperament claim.

VBO:0200894.summary: Miniature Pinschers are lively, spirited and self-assured, yet tend to keep an even temperament. They were already kept in large numbers around the turn of the twentieth century; Germany’s 1925 stud book recorded at least 1,300 entries, a measure of how established this small companion breed had become.
VBO:0200894.shortDescription: A lively, self-assured small Pinscher with an even temperament and a long German breed history.
VBO:0200894.historicalRoots: German Miniature Pinscher, numerous by the early twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI standard 185, Miniature Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI 185 describes lively, spirited, self-assured and evenly tempered character; notes large numbers around 1900 and more than 1,300 stud-book entries in 1925. Black-and-tan is an accepted color, not a temperament distinction.

VBO:0200940.summary: Brown Newfoundlands share the breed’s notable gentleness and serenity, along with a joyful, dignified character. On the island of Newfoundland, dogs of this type hauled heavy loads on land and worked in cold water; their strength and composure also made them lifeguards for people facing rough seas.
VBO:0200940.shortDescription: A gentle, serene brown Newfoundland rooted in heavy hauling and cold-water rescue work.
VBO:0200940.historicalRoots: Island of Newfoundland working water dog and heavy-load hauler.

sources.title: FCI standard 50, Newfoundland
sources.evidence: FCI 50 describes dignified, joyful, gentle and serene temperament; traces island of Newfoundland history, heavy sledge loads, water work and lifeguard use. Brown is a recognized coat color.

VBO:0201093.summary: Black Pugs are even-tempered, happy and lively companions with a dignified manner. The breed moved from China through Dutch traders into European courts; black dogs were introduced to England in 1877, after a period when only fawn Pugs had been recorded there.
VBO:0201093.shortDescription: A happy, even-tempered black Pug, part of a companion breed long admired in China and Europe.
VBO:0201093.historicalRoots: Companion breed listed from China, spread to Europe through Dutch traders; black Pugs recorded in England from 1877.

sources.title: FCI standard 253, Pug
sources.evidence: FCI 253 describes charm, dignity, intelligence, even temperament and a happy lively disposition; recounts the China–Dutch–England route and black pair introduced in England in 1877.

VBO:0200592.summary: Medium German Spitz are attentive and lively, strongly attached to familiar people and quick to learn. Their traditional watch-and-companion role draws on natural reserve toward strangers and little hunting drive, traits that have made them alert around homes and farms in Central Europe.
VBO:0200592.shortDescription: An attentive, lively medium German Spitz with a watchful streak and strong attachment.
VBO:0200592.historicalRoots: Central European German Spitz watch-and-companion tradition.

sources.title: FCI standard 97, German Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI 97 German Giant/Medium/Miniature section describes attentive, lively, attached, teachable behavior, reserve toward strangers, little hunting instinct and home/farm watchdog use; medium height 35±5 cm and orange-sable as an accepted other color.

VBO:0200593.summary: White Medium German Spitz are attentive, lively companions with marked attachment to familiar people and a readily teachable nature. Their old home-and-farm watchdog role drew on alertness and natural reserve around strangers, while a limited hunting drive distinguished that work from pursuit in the field.
VBO:0200593.shortDescription: A lively, attached white medium German Spitz with a watchful home-and-farm heritage.
VBO:0200593.historicalRoots: Central European German Spitz watch-and-companion tradition.

sources.title: FCI standard 97, German Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI 97 Giant/Medium/Miniature section describes attentive, lively, attached, teachable behavior, stranger reserve, lack of hunting instinct and home/farm watchdog use; medium height 35±5 cm and pure white coat accepted.

VBO:0200595.summary: Brown Miniature German Spitz are lively and attentive, with strong attachment to familiar people and a teachable nature. Even in a smaller frame, they retain the old German Spitz watch-and-companion role around home and farm, where natural reserve toward strangers matters more than a hunting drive.
VBO:0200595.shortDescription: A lively, attached brown Miniature Spitz with a watchful home-and-farm heritage.
VBO:0200595.historicalRoots: Central European German Spitz, miniature watch-and-companion variety.

sources.title: FCI standard 97, German Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI 97 Giant/Medium/Miniature section describes lively, attentive, attached, teachable character, stranger reserve, little hunting instinct and home/farm watchdog use; Miniature Spitz height 27±3 cm and uniformly dark brown recognized.

VBO:0200597.summary: White Miniature German Spitz are attentive and lively, with marked attachment to familiar people and a willingness to learn. Their old watch-and-companion role around home and farm drew on natural reserve toward strangers; the breed has little hunting drive and is known for staying alert to its surroundings.
VBO:0200597.shortDescription: A lively, attentive white Miniature Spitz with strong attachment and a watchful nature.
VBO:0200597.historicalRoots: Central European German Spitz, miniature watch-and-companion variety.

sources.title: FCI standard 97, German Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI 97 Giant/Medium/Miniature section describes attentive, lively, attached and teachable character, stranger reserve, little hunting instinct and home/farm watch use; miniature height 27±3 cm and pure white accepted.

VBO:0200417.summary: Smooth-haired Dachshunds are friendly and even-tempered, but their hunting style is persistent and quick, guided by an excellent nose. Descended from short-legged Bracken, the Dachshund has worked both above and below ground since its medieval roots; the smooth-coated form carries that versatile hunting tradition.
VBO:0200417.shortDescription: A friendly, persistent smooth-haired Dachshund bred to track and hunt above and below ground.
VBO:0200417.historicalRoots: German Dachshund bred from short-legged Bracken for underground and above-ground hunting.

sources.title: FCI standard 148, Dachshund
sources.evidence: FCI 148 records friendly/even temperament, passionate persistent fast hunting and excellent nose; traces Dachshund to Middle Ages and short-legged Bracken, with use above and below ground; smooth coat is short, dense and close.

VBO:0200482.summary: Bull Terriers are spirited, fun-loving dogs whose courage and occasional stubbornness sit beside an even temperament. James Hinks established the recognizable breed type in mid-nineteenth-century Britain, and Bull Terriers appeared at Birmingham shows by 1862. The standard expects a dog that can respond to discipline and enjoy people.
VBO:0200482.shortDescription: A spirited British terrier with a playful side, resolve and a nineteenth-century show history.
VBO:0200482.historicalRoots: British Bull Terrier standardized by James Hinks in the 1850s and shown at Birmingham in 1862.

sources.title: FCI standard 11
sources.evidence: FCI 11 describes the Bull Terrier as courageous, spirited, fun-loving, even-tempered and amenable to discipline, though sometimes obstinate and especially good with people. Its history names James Hinks as standardizing the type in the 1850s and records its 1862 Birmingham showing.

VBO:0200483.summary: Bull Terriers are bold and full of spirit, with a playful nature that can coexist with a stubborn streak. The breed's British standard asks for an even temperament and responsiveness to discipline. James Hinks formalized the type in the 1850s, and a Bull Terrier Club followed in 1887.
VBO:0200483.shortDescription: A bold, playful British terrier whose determined character calls for steady guidance.
VBO:0200483.historicalRoots: Mid-nineteenth-century British standardization by James Hinks; Bull Terrier Club formed in 1887.

sources.title: FCI standard 11
sources.evidence: FCI 11 describes a spirited, fun-loving yet even-tempered dog, amenable to discipline despite possible obstinacy. Its history credits James Hinks with standardizing the type in the 1850s and dates the Bull Terrier Club to 1887.

VBO:0200561.summary: Great Gascon Saintongeois are calm, affectionate pack hounds with fine noses, a wide-ranging search and a ringing voice. Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour developed the breed in nineteenth-century France by crossing the last Saintonge hounds with Bleu de Gascogne stock. Its larger form still serves in pack hunting of big game and hare.
VBO:0200561.shortDescription: A calm, fine-nosed French pack hound bred for wide searches and a ringing voice.
VBO:0200561.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century French crossing of Saintonge hounds and Bleu de Gascogne stock.

sources.title: FCI standard 21
sources.evidence: FCI 21 describes both Gascon Saintongeois forms as fine-nosed, wide-casting, sonorous pack hounds that are calm, affectionate and amenable to orders. The Great form came from Count de Carayon-Latour crossing the last Saintonge hounds with Bleu de Gascogne stock in the nineteenth century; utilization includes big game and hare.

VBO:0200562.summary: Small Gascon Saintongeois share the larger hound's calm, affectionate pack instinct, fine nose and sonorous voice. Hunters in southwest France selected smaller dogs from Great Gascon Saintongeois litters in the mid-twentieth century for hare work. The standard also recognizes this medium-sized hound as capable on bigger game.
VBO:0200562.shortDescription: A calm French pack hound bred from smaller Great Gascon dogs for hare hunting in southwest France.
VBO:0200562.historicalRoots: Southwest French selection of smaller Great Gascon Saintongeois for hare hunting in the mid-twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI standard 21
sources.evidence: FCI 21 describes both forms as calm, affectionate, fine-nosed, wide-casting pack hounds with a sonorous voice. Hunters in southwest France selected the smallest dogs from Great Gascon Saintongeois litters in the mid-twentieth century for hare hunting; the Small form also works larger game.

VBO:0201005.summary: Peruvian Hairless Dogs are lively, alert companions, affectionate with familiar people and sometimes wary of strangers. Their watchful role has endured alongside a much older cultural presence: the breed appears in ceramics from several pre-Inca societies. Official recognition in 1985 gave this native breed a modern standard.
VBO:0201005.shortDescription: A lively, affectionate Peruvian companion with watchful instincts and pre-Inca roots.
VBO:0201005.historicalRoots: Pre-Inca Peruvian ceramics, followed by modern recognition of the native breed in 1985.

sources.title: FCI standard 310
sources.evidence: FCI 310 calls the Peruvian Hairless Dog lively and alert, affectionate with close people, possibly wary of strangers and a good watchdog. Its history records depictions in several pre-Inca cultures’ ceramics and recognition as a native Peruvian breed in 1985; the large size is one of three classes.

VBO:0201006.summary: Peruvian Hairless Dogs tend to be lively and alert yet affectionate with those close to them, and may hold back around strangers. Their role as watchful companions is documented in the breed standard. Peruvian ceramics from several pre-Inca cultures show the hairless dog, a record much older than its official 1985 recognition.
VBO:0201006.shortDescription: An alert, affectionate Peruvian companion that may be reserved with unfamiliar people.
VBO:0201006.historicalRoots: Pre-Inca Peruvian cultural record; modern FCI recognition of the native breed in 1985.

sources.title: FCI standard 310
sources.evidence: FCI 310 describes a lively, alert dog affectionate with close people, possibly wary of strangers and watchful at home. It documents hairless dogs in pre-Inca Peruvian ceramics and official native-breed recognition in 1985; medium is one of three size classes.

VBO:0201437.summary: Intermediate Xoloitzcuintles share the breed's quiet, calm manner, cheerful alertness and tendency to watch strangers carefully. The Mexican standard assigns the intermediate size a watchdog role. This native breed came close to disappearing before the Mexican Kennel Club helped restore it and adopted its image as a logo in 1940.
VBO:0201437.shortDescription: A calm, watchful Mexican dog whose native breed was rescued from near extinction.
VBO:0201437.historicalRoots: Ancient Mexican native breed preserved after a period of near extinction; Mexican Kennel Club logo since 1940.

sources.title: FCI standard 234
sources.evidence: FCI 234 describes the Xoloitzcuintle as quiet, calm, cheerful and alert, potentially suspicious of strangers, with Intermediate and Standard sizes used as watchdogs. Its history says the breed became scarce and the Mexican Kennel Club rescued it, using its image as a logo from 1940.

VBO:0201439.summary: Standard Xoloitzcuintles are quiet, alert companions whose watchful reserve toward strangers suits the standard size's watchdog role. The breed has deep roots in pre-Hispanic Mexico, where it appeared in ritual belief as a guide for souls. It later became scarce, and the Mexican Kennel Club helped preserve it in the twentieth century.
VBO:0201439.shortDescription: A quiet, alert Mexican watchdog with a long place in pre-Hispanic ritual tradition.
VBO:0201439.historicalRoots: Pre-Hispanic Mexican ritual tradition; preservation by the Mexican Kennel Club.

sources.title: FCI standard 234
sources.evidence: FCI 234 assigns the Standard size a watchdog role and describes a quiet, calm, cheerful, alert breed that may be suspicious of strangers. Its historical summary records pre-Hispanic Mexican belief in the dog as a guide for souls, later scarcity and rescue by the Mexican Kennel Club.

VBO:0200409.summary: Miniature Long-Haired Dachshunds share the breed's friendly, even temper and persistent nose for a trail. Dachshunds were bred from German scenthounds for hunting both below and above ground, where they flush game and follow wounded animals.
VBO:0200409.shortDescription: A friendly, persistent little trail-follower from Germany's above- and below-ground hunting line.
VBO:0200409.historicalRoots: German Dachshund hunting tradition; miniature longhaired size-and-coat variety.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 148: Dachshund
sources.evidence: FCI describes friendly, even temperament, passionate and persistent scent work, above- and below-ground hunting, flushing and wounded-game tracking; it recognizes Miniature Long-Haired as one of nine size/coat combinations. No coat-specific character claim.

VBO:0200410.summary: Miniature Smooth-Haired Dachshunds are friendly, even-tempered little dogs with a persistent nose for a trail. The Dachshund was developed to follow scent below ground and still works above ground by flushing and tracking wounded game.
VBO:0200410.shortDescription: A small smooth-coated Dachshund with an even nature and the breed's persistent tracking drive.
VBO:0200410.historicalRoots: German Dachshund tradition, adapted for scent work below and above ground.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 148: Dachshund
sources.evidence: FCI recognizes the Miniature Smooth-Haired size/coat combination, friendly/even breed temperament, persistent nose, underground hunting, flushing and wounded-game tracking. No smooth-coat-specific behavioral claim.

VBO:0201252.summary: Small Bernese Hounds are friendly, determined scenthounds with a melodious voice on a trail. They were bred when larger Swiss Hounds were judged too fast for enclosed hunting grounds, and the smaller dogs kept a keen nose for searching difficult terrain and following wounded game.
VBO:0201252.shortDescription: A friendly, determined Swiss trail hound bred for smaller hunting grounds and a singing voice.
VBO:0201252.historicalRoots: Swiss short-legged hound selected for enclosed hunting grounds around the turn of the twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 60: Swiss Short-Legged Hound
sources.evidence: FCI traces shorter hounds to enclosed Swiss hunting grounds, describes friendly character, determined solo scent work with melodious cry and wounded-game tracking, and identifies the black-white-tan Small Bernese color and smooth coat.

VBO:0201074.summary: Large Portuguese Podengos are lively, intelligent hunters traditionally used on big game. The breed also serves as a watchdog and companion. Its ancestry is thought to run back to dogs brought to Iberia in classical antiquity, then shaped over centuries by Portuguese terrain and climate.
VBO:0201074.shortDescription: A lively, intelligent large Portuguese hunting dog traditionally used on big game and as a watchful companion.
VBO:0201074.historicalRoots: Portuguese Podengo hunting tradition; large variety used on big game.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 94: Podengo Português
sources.evidence: FCI gives the large variety big-game use, watch/companion roles, lively intelligent breed character, and cautiously says the primitive type probably descends from dogs brought to Iberia by Phoenicians and Romans in classical antiquity, later adapting to Portuguese terrain and climate. It also gives large size and allowed smooth fawn coat.

VBO:0201075.summary: Medium Portuguese Podengos are lively, intelligent rabbit hunters that can work alone or with a pack. The breed is also traditionally used as a watchdog and kept as a companion, but its warren-hound name points to that distinctive field skill.
VBO:0201075.shortDescription: A lively medium Portuguese rabbit hunter that can follow a warren alone or work with a pack.
VBO:0201075.historicalRoots: Portuguese warren-hound tradition; medium Podengo used for rabbit hunting.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 94: Podengo Português
sources.evidence: FCI gives the medium variety rabbit-hunting work alone or in pack, breed-wide watch/companion roles and lively intelligent character; medium 40–54 cm and wire beard. Exact medium wire-haired caption on source page.
